quote: Uebt das geometrische Zeichnen die geometrische An- schauung so sehr? und nicht vielmehr
english: Does geometric drawing train geometric intuition so much? and not rather
topic: Loose reflections: a soldier's respect for a commander who shoots well, the inessential nature of words compared with the thought as 'invariant', whether practical activities such as gardening give better knowledge of geometric concepts, how interests in the same object differ, and whether geometric drawing trains geometric intuition.

triage.modern_statement: This is not a mathematical research question. It is a question about teaching and psychology: does practice in geometric (technical) drawing do much to develop geometric or spatial intuition (Anschauung), or does something else do more? The sentence breaks off at 'and not rather', so the alternative Hilbert had in mind isn't recorded. The page context suggests it was practical, hands-on activity such as gardening. In modern terms this is roughly the question studied in education and cognitive psychology of whether training in drawing or technical drawing improves spatial visualization ability.
triage.answered_by: Not a mathematical problem, so no mathematical answer exists. The nearest modern equivalent is empirical work on spatial-ability training. For example, a 2018 study in Cognitive Processing (Springer, 'Spatial Visualization ability improves with and without studying Technical Drawing') found that spatial visualization improves whether or not students study technical drawing. A 2023 study in Memory & Cognition found no significant effect of fine-arts or drawing training on spatial-ability tasks, though posttest effect sizes slightly favored the origami and drawing groups. Neither study refers to Hilbert's note.

evidence.claim: Research on technical drawing and spatial visualization reports that spatial visualization ability improves both with and without studying technical drawing. Studying subjects such as technical drawing or geometry is described as training spatial ability indirectly.
A study of fine-arts training found no significant interaction between training group and time point for spatial-ability tasks, although posttest effect sizes favored the origami and drawing groups.

Hilbert's interest in geometric intuition later appeared in published form in Hilbert & Cohn-Vossen, 'Anschauliche Geometrie' (Geometry and the Imagination). This shows his general interest in intuition, not an answer to this note.

triage.why: The note is one of several loose reflections on the same page, alongside a soldier's respect for a commander, words versus thought, and gardening. It asks a teaching and psychology question, not a mathematical one, and it is cut off before the alternative is stated. It is not among the 23 problems or the 24th problem, and I found no source discussing this specific note. Empirical research on whether drawing or technical-drawing training improves spatial ability does exist and is still being published (2018, 2023), with mixed results. But that research is educational psychology, not mathematics, so 'active_today' is left as unclear for mathematics. Confidence is high that this is not a research question. The sources only show related modern work, not anything connected to Hilbert's note.
